entries.title: How the gland is built
entries.text: Orientation: four hormones, two control systems The three stated objectives, and how this page delivers them 1. Associate symptoms, signs, and diagnostic findings with the underlying disorder — the aldosterone , cortisol excess , insufficiency , CAH , neoplasm , pheochromocytoma , and MEN sections, each written presentation-first. 2. Prescribe the correct first-line diagnostic test — every disorder names its own first test, and one table collects all of them so you can rehearse the choice in isolation. 3. Discuss management of primary, secondary, and tertiary causes based on case characteristics and test results — the management section , plus adrenal crisis , which is the one you must be able to do without looking anything up. Cortex — three zones Glomerulosa → aldosterone , answering to angiotensin II and potassium. Fasciculata → cortisol , answering to ACTH. Reticularis → DHEA and androstenedione , also ACTH-responsive. The synthetic pathway itself is worked through on the steroid synthesis page . Medulla — a different organ Neural-crest-derived chromaffin cells making catecholamines . Not part of the steroid story at all, not under ACTH control, and the source of pheochromocytoma . It is inside the same capsule; that is the whole relationship. The two questions to ask every time Which hormone, and in which direction? That names the syndrome. Gland or signal? That names the level — primary means the gland, secondary means the pituitary, tertiary means the hypothalamus, and for aldosterone "secondary" means the renin–angiotensin system is driving it. Cortisol read against ACTH — a four-box localizer A two-by-two grid. High cortisol with low ACTH indicates an adrenal source or exogenous glucocorticoid. High cortisol with high or normal ACTH indicates Cushing disease from a pituitary adenoma or ectopic ACTH secretion. Low cortisol with high ACTH indicates primary adrenal insufficiency. Low cortisol with low or normal ACTH indicates central adrenal insufficiency. The rule is that hormone and trophic signal moving in opposite directions localizes the fault to the gland, while moving in the same direction localizes it above the gland. Read cortisol against ACTH ACTH low or normal ACTH high Cortisol high Cortisol low ACTH-independent Cushing syndrome adrenal adenoma or carcinoma, bilateral hyperplasia — or exogenous glucocorticoid, which is by far the commonest cause Central adrenal insufficiency secondary (pituitary) or tertiary (hypothalamic) aldosterone spared · no pigment ACTH-dependent Cushing syndrome pituitary adenoma = Cushing disease, or ectopic ACTH high-dose dexamethasone splits them Primary adrenal insufficiency Addison disease and the rest aldosterone lost too · hyperpigmented · hyperkalemic opposite directions → the gland is the problem · same direction → the problem is above the gland Original diagram. The identical logic applied to aldosterone and renin gives you the hyperaldosteronism split: aldosterone high with renin suppressed is primary, both high is secondary. One rule, two axes, most of this lecture.

entries.title: Hyperaldosteronism
entries.text: Hyperaldosteronism, primary and secondary The commonest secondary cause of hypertension, and routinely missed because the potassium is often normal. What aldosterone does, so you can predict the syndrome Aldosterone acts on the principal cells of the distal nephron : it upregulates the Na⁺/K⁺-ATPase and the epithelial sodium channel, so sodium is retained, water follows, and potassium and hydrogen ions are excreted . Predict from that: hypertension from volume expansion, hypokalemia , and a metabolic alkalosis . Sodium is often near-normal because water is retained alongside it. It is normally released in response to angiotensin II (that is, to low renal perfusion or low blood pressure) and to high serum potassium ; ACTH contributes to a minor extent. Primary — the adrenal is autonomous Aldosterone is high and renin is suppressed , because the volume expansion shuts the renin–angiotensin system off and the gland ignores it anyway. Causes: bilateral adrenocortical hyperplasia (idiopathic hyperaldosteronism, the commonest), an aldosterone-producing adenoma — Conn syndrome , rarely an adrenocortical carcinoma , and the familial forms including glucocorticoid-remediable aldosteronism . Symptoms are those of hypertension plus those of hypokalemia — weakness, paresthesias, tetany, visual disturbance, polyuria — and in a great many patients, nothing at all. Secondary — the signal is driving it Aldosterone is high and renin is high too , because the adrenal is responding correctly to an abnormal stimulus. Anything that reduces renal perfusion will do it: renal artery stenosis or atheroma , renal vasoconstriction as in accelerated hypertension, and the edematous states — heart failure, cirrhosis with ascites, nephrotic syndrome. Renin is the single value that separates the two , which is why the screening test is a ratio and not an aldosterone level. Who to screen — a high index of suspicion Test for primary aldosteronism in: sustained blood pressure above 150/100 on three measurements on three different days; hypertension above 140/90 resistant to three agents ; controlled hypertension requiring four or more agents ; hypertension with hypokalemia — whether spontaneous or diuretic-induced; hypertension with an adrenal incidentaloma ; hypertension with obstructive sleep apnea ; hypertension with a family history of early-onset hypertension or of stroke before 40 ; and hypertension in anyone with a first-degree relative who has primary aldosteronism . Note that normal potassium does not exclude it — hypokalemia is present in a minority. Funder JW et al. The Management of Primary Aldosteronism: Case Detection, Diagnosis, and Treatment: An Endocrine Society Clinical Practice Guideline. J Clin Endocrinol Metab 2016;101(5):1889–1916. academic.oup.com/jcem/article/101/5/1889

entries.title: Cushing syndrome
entries.text: Cushing syndrome and Cushing disease Two terms that are not interchangeable, and the distinction is examinable. Get the vocabulary right first Cushing syndrome is the whole clinical picture produced by inappropriately high exposure to glucocorticoid, from any source. Cushing disease is the specific subset caused by an ACTH-secreting pituitary adenoma . Every Cushing disease is a Cushing syndrome; most Cushing syndrome is not Cushing disease. And the commonest cause of the syndrome overall is not a tumour at all — it is exogenous glucocorticoid therapy . The features, and the mechanism behind each Central obesity with thin extremities — cortisol is catabolic and an insulin antagonist: it mobilizes peripheral fat and breaks down muscle while promoting visceral fat deposition. Thin, easily bruised skin and wide purple striae — impaired collagen synthesis and abnormal wound healing. Facial plethora — dilated facial capillaries under thinned skin. Proximal muscle weakness — the same catabolism. Secondary hypertension — cortisol potentiates the vasoconstrictor effect of catecholamines, and at high concentrations it also spills onto the mineralocorticoid receptor. Hyperglycemia and diabetes, hypertriglyceridemia — insulin resistance. Osteoporosis , immunosuppression , mood disturbance , and hypogonadism , because cortisol suppresses gonadotropins. In children the presentation is different The single most useful pediatric sign is growth failure with weight gain — a child crossing height percentiles downward while crossing weight percentiles upward . Almost nothing else does that. Obesity alone in a child is usually exogenous and comes with accelerated growth; it is the combination that should prompt testing. When to raise your index of suspicion Test people with features unusual for their age — hypertension, osteoporosis, type 2 diabetes, or thin skin in a young adult; people with multiple and progressive features rather than one in isolation; children with a falling height percentile and a rising weight percentile ; and people with an adrenal incidentaloma . The reason for the threshold is that individual features — obesity, hypertension, glucose intolerance — are extremely common in the general population and testing everybody produces mostly false positives.

entries.title: Primary adrenal insufficiency
entries.text: Primary adrenal insufficiency Described by Thomas Addison in 1855. Progressive destruction of the adrenal cortex — so both cortisol and aldosterone are lost. Predict every symptom from the two missing hormones Missing cortisol: fatigue, anorexia, weight loss, nausea and vomiting, abdominal pain, apathy and confusion, hypoglycemia , and an inability to withstand physiological stress. Missing aldosterone: sodium wasting → hyponatremia , hypovolemia , postural hypotension , tachycardia, salt craving , and — because potassium is no longer excreted — hyperkalemia , often with a mild metabolic acidosis. The one finding that is not a deficiency at all: hyperpigmentation , most obvious in palmar creases, buccal mucosa, scars, and pressure areas. It is caused by the excess ACTH and related POMC-derived peptides, and it is the physical sign that tells you the problem is primary rather than central. In neonates, prolonged jaundice belongs on the list too. Causes — autoimmune leads in high-income countries Autoimmune adrenalitis (Addison disease) , with 21-hydroxylase antibodies , often as part of an autoimmune polyglandular syndrome — which is why a patient recently started on levothyroxine who then deteriorates deserves a second look. Infection — tuberculosis, which remains the leading cause worldwide; disseminated fungal disease; HIV-associated disease; and Waterhouse-Friderichsen syndrome . Infiltration — amyloidosis, sarcoidosis, hemochromatosis, metastases. Genetic — congenital adrenal hypoplasia (DAX1/NR0B1, SF1/NR5A1, ACTH-receptor mutations) and adrenoleukodystrophy . Metabolic and drug-related — congenital adrenal hyperplasia, and drugs that inhibit steroidogenesis. Adrenoleukodystrophy — worth knowing separately An X-linked peroxisomal disorder (ABCD1) in which very long chain fatty acids accumulate in the brain, adrenal cortex, and testicular Leydig cells . It can present as isolated adrenal insufficiency years before neurological disease, so every boy with primary adrenal insufficiency and no antibodies needs a VLCFA level . It was added to the US Recommended Uniform Screening Panel in 2016, so most children in the United States are now screened at birth. Waterhouse-Friderichsen syndrome fulminant adrenal hemorrhage in sepsis Emergency The picture Overwhelming bacterial sepsis — classically Neisseria meningitidis — with rapidly progressive hypotension and shock , disseminated intravascular coagulation with purpura , and massive bilateral adrenal hemorrhage producing acute adrenocortical insufficiency. More common in children. If the infection is not treated within hours, death follows in hours to days. The pathology The mechanism of the hemorrhage is not settled; bacterial seeding of small adrenal vessels with endotoxin-induced vasculitis is the usual explanation. Macroscopically the glands are hemorrhagic sacs and the cortical architecture is indiscernible . What you actually do Antibiotics and resuscitation immediately, and stress-dose hydrocortisone without waiting for a cortisol result . This is the classic acute presentation of primary adrenal failure and the reason "treat first, confirm later" is the rule in adrenal crisis .

entries.title: Secondary and tertiary AI
entries.text: Central adrenal insufficiency — secondary and tertiary What is different, and why Any disorder of the pituitary or hypothalamus that reduces ACTH gives low ACTH with low cortisol . The critical difference from primary disease is that aldosterone is normal , because the zona glomerulosa answers to the renin–angiotensin system and to potassium, not to ACTH. Therefore: no hyperkalemia, no salt craving, no mineralocorticoid replacement needed . And no excess ACTH means no hyperpigmentation . Hyponatremia can still occur, because cortisol normally restrains vasopressin release. Causes Withdrawal of exogenous glucocorticoid therapy — by a wide margin the commonest cause of central adrenal insufficiency, and the reason chronic steroids are tapered rather than stopped. Hypopituitarism from any cause — tumour, surgery, radiation, apoplexy, infiltration. Hypothalamic disease — tumour, radiation, surgery (this is the tertiary form). Isolated ACTH deficiency , and defects in POMC , which characteristically also give red hair and early obesity. Primary versus central at a glance Both: low cortisol, fatigue, weight loss, hypoglycemia, hyponatremia. Primary only: high ACTH, hyperpigmentation, low aldosterone with high renin, hyperkalemia, salt craving, and a need for fludrocortisone. Central only: low ACTH, other pituitary hormone deficits, and often a history of exogenous steroids.

entries.title: Congenital adrenal hyperplasia
entries.text: Congenital adrenal hyperplasia A group of autosomal recessive loss-of-function disorders of the steroidogenic enzymes. The mechanism is derived step by step on the steroid synthesis page ; here it is the clinical face. The shape of the disease An enzyme in the cortisol pathway is deficient → cortisol falls → ACTH rises → the adrenals become bilaterally hyperplastic, up to 10–15 times normal weight → precursors above the block accumulate and are shunted into whichever branch is still open . In the commonest form that branch is the androgens. 21-hydroxylase deficiency accounts for 90–95% of cases. In the severe form both cortisol and aldosterone are lost, so infants present with adrenal and salt-wasting crisis : poor feeding, vomiting, failure to thrive, dehydration, hyponatremia, hyperkalemia, hypoglycemia, and shock , typically at 1 to 3 weeks of age . 46,XX infants have atypical genitalia; 46,XY infants may look entirely normal — which is precisely why the newborn screen exists. The four blocks compared. Read each row across and the phenotype falls out of the biochemistry. Deficiency ACTH Cortisol 17-OHP Aldosterone DOC Androgens Genitalia 21-hydroxylase (90–95%) High Low High Low Low High 46,XX virilized · salt wasting 11β-hydroxylase High Low Normal Low High High 46,XX virilized · hypertension 17α-hydroxylase / 17,20-lyase High Low Low Normal High Low 46,XY undervirilized · hypertension · absent puberty 3β-HSD High Low Normal Low Normal High (weak — DHEA) Either sex can be atypical The two hypertensive forms, and why the aldosterone value looks wrong In both 11β-hydroxylase and 17α-hydroxylase deficiency, measured aldosterone is low but the patient is hypertensive and hypokalemic . That is not a contradiction: 11-deoxycorticosterone accumulates above the block , and DOC is a weak mineralocorticoid present in large enough quantities to act like a strong one. The excess mineralocorticoid activity then suppresses renin, and low renin suppresses aldosterone. Hypertension in a child with CAH means DOC , and it is the finding that separates these two from 21-hydroxylase deficiency at the bedside.

entries.title: The virilized child
entries.text: Working up virilization in a child A common presentation with a short and orderly differential. The differential, roughly in order Idiopathic — the commonest. Premature adrenarche — early pubic and axillary hair from early maturation of the zona reticularis, without other pubertal signs. Insulin resistance and PCOS . Congenital adrenal hyperplasia , including the non-classic form. An adrenal or gonadal tumour — suspect this when onset is rapid, virilization is severe, or the androgen levels are extreme. Iatrogenic androgen exposure , which is easy to miss and free to ask about. First-line tests, and reading them 17-hydroxyprogesterone (early morning) — high points to CAH. DHEA-S — the adrenal androgen marker; a markedly raised value, of the order of ten times the upper limit, points to an adrenal tumour rather than hyperplasia. Androstenedione and testosterone — a very high testosterone with a normal DHEA-S points to a gonadal source. Add bone age, and imaging directed by the biochemistry.

entries.title: Adrenocortical neoplasms
entries.text: Adrenocortical neoplasms Adenoma and carcinoma differ on almost every axis, which is what makes the imaging phenotype so useful. Adenoma Carcinoma Function Non-functional in roughly 60%; may make cortisol, aldosterone, or sex steroids Typically functional — often virilization or a mixed hormone picture How it is found Usually incidental , on imaging done for another reason Symptomatic — a hormonal syndrome, a mass effect, or systemic illness Size and margins Well circumscribed, usually up to about 2.5 cm Large and invasive , frequently well over 10 cm Adjacent cortex Normal thickness Atrophic , suppressed by the tumour's own output Spread None Regional and para-aortic nodes; hematogenous spread to lung , liver, bone Inherited associations — Li-Fraumeni (TP53) and Beckwith-Wiedemann The incidentaloma — two questions, always both Is it functioning? Screen every adrenal incidentaloma with a 1 mg overnight dexamethasone suppression test and plasma or urinary metanephrines , and add an aldosterone-to-renin ratio if the patient is hypertensive or hypokalemic . Is it malignant? Judge from size and imaging phenotype — a small, homogeneous, lipid-rich lesion with low attenuation on unenhanced CT behaves like an adenoma, whereas a large, heterogeneous, irregular lesion does not. Biopsy is not the first move, and must never be done before pheochromocytoma has been excluded biochemically.

entries.title: Pheochromocytoma
entries.text: Pheochromocytoma and paraganglioma A catecholamine-secreting tumour of the adrenal medulla. Outside the medulla the same tumour is called a paraganglioma. The presentation The classic triad is headache, diaphoresis, and palpitations , occurring in episodes that wax and wane. The commonest single finding is hypertension — which may be sustained, paroxysmal, or both, and is often severe. Add pallor, tremor, anxiety, and hyperglycemia. A young or middle-aged patient with resistant or episodic hypertension is the person to think of it in. Paraganglioma and the genetics Paragangliomas arise from extra-adrenal chromaffin tissue and are strongly associated with mutations of the succinate dehydrogenase (SDHx) genes, of which SDHB carries the highest risk of metastatic disease. Every patient should be referred for genetic testing — a large minority of these tumours are germline — and the syndromes to know are MEN2A and MEN2B (RET), von Hippel-Lindau (VHL), neurofibromatosis type 1 (NF1), and the hereditary paraganglioma syndromes (SDHx). Up to 20–25% become metastatic , so surveillance is lifelong. One correction worth making against the slide set The lecture lists Sturge-Weber syndrome among the syndromic associations of pheochromocytoma. The associations consistently reported in the literature are MEN2, VHL, NF1, and the SDHx paraganglioma syndromes ; Sturge-Weber is not an established one. Learn the four — they are the ones a question will test, and they are the ones that determine which gene panel is sent.

entries.title: MEN syndromes
entries.text: The multiple endocrine neoplasia syndromes All three are autosomal dominant. Two genes cover all of them: MEN1 for type 1, RET for both type 2 syndromes. The MEN syndromes side by side. Medullary thyroid carcinoma is in both type 2 syndromes and neither type 1 tumour set; hyperparathyroidism is in MEN1 and MEN2A but not MEN2B. MEN1 MEN2A MEN2B Gene MEN1 , a tumour suppressor encoding menin RET proto-oncogene RET proto-oncogene (classically M918T) Core tumours The three Ps — P arathyroid, P ituitary, P ancreas Medullary thyroid carcinoma , pheochromocytoma , hyperparathyroidism Medullary thyroid carcinoma , pheochromocytoma (~50%) — no hyperparathyroidism Commonest first manifestation Primary hyperparathyroidism in 80–95%, and at a much younger age than sporadic disease — around 25 rather than 55 Medullary thyroid carcinoma Medullary thyroid carcinoma, earlier and more aggressive than in 2A Other features Pituitary: prolactinoma , GH-secreting adenoma. Pancreas: gastrinoma (Zollinger-Ellison), insulinoma Cutaneous lichen amyloidosis and Hirschsprung disease Mucocutaneous neuromas , marfanoid habitus with joint laxity and skeletal deformity, myelinated corneal nerves , intestinal ganglioneuromatosis A distinction the slide set blurs The slides place Hirschsprung disease in the MEN2B column alongside intestinal ganglioneuromas. The published association is the other way round: Hirschsprung disease goes with MEN2A (typically RET exon 10 variants), while diffuse intestinal ganglioneuromatosis is the MEN2B feature . The two are opposite lesions of the enteric nervous system — absent ganglion cells in Hirschsprung, excess ganglion cells in ganglioneuromatosis — which is a good way to keep them apart. Cutaneous lichen amyloidosis is a MEN2A feature (classically codon 634). What a MEN2 diagnosis obliges you to do Medullary thyroid carcinoma arises from parafollicular C cells and secretes calcitonin , which is its tumour marker. Because penetrance approaches 100%, RET carriers are offered prophylactic thyroidectomy , timed by the specific variant's risk. Pheochromocytoma requires lifelong surveillance with plasma or urinary metanephrines, and must be excluded and treated before any other surgery — operating on an unblocked pheochromocytoma can precipitate a hypertensive crisis. Hyperparathyroidism in MEN2A is followed with calcium and PTH.

entries.title: Localize from the labs
entries.text: Localize the lesion Seven patterns. This is the skill objective 1 is really asking for.

entries.title: First-line test for each
entries.text: The correct first test, disorder by disorder Objective 2 in one table. Learn the first column against the second; the third column is what you do when the first test is positive. Screening tests are chosen for sensitivity; confirmatory tests for specificity. Do not skip straight to imaging — a mass does not prove function, and function does not require a visible mass. Suspected disorder First-line test Then what Primary aldosteronism Aldosterone-to-renin ratio under standard conditions Confirmatory testing (oral salt loading, saline infusion, fludrocortisone suppression, or captopril challenge) — which may be omitted with spontaneous hypokalemia, undetectable renin, and aldosterone above 20 ng/dL . Then adrenal CT in everyone , and adrenal vein sampling to separate unilateral from bilateral disease whenever surgery is on the table. AVS beats CT here: small adenomas are missed and non-functioning nodules mislead. Cushing syndrome Any one of: late-night salivary cortisol , 24-hour urinary free cortisol , or a 1 mg overnight dexamethasone suppression test — usually two of them, abnormal, before proceeding Then plasma ACTH to split ACTH-dependent from ACTH-independent disease. If ACTH-dependent, a high-dose dexamethasone suppression test and pituitary MRI: a pituitary adenoma suppresses, ectopic ACTH does not . Inferior petrosal sinus sampling settles ambiguous cases. Adrenal insufficiency Early-morning cortisol with a simultaneous ACTH ACTH (cosyntropin) stimulation test — 250 µg, with cortisol at 30 and 60 minutes; a peak below roughly 18 µg/dL is diagnostic on traditional assays. Then localize: high ACTH = primary (add renin, aldosterone, 21-hydroxylase antibodies , and VLCFA in a male), low or normal ACTH = central (image the pituitary, check the other axes). Congenital adrenal hyperplasia 17-hydroxyprogesterone — on the newborn screen, or an early-morning level later in life Electrolytes, glucose, renin, and cortisol; ACTH stimulation if the value is equivocal, as it often is in the non-classic form; genotyping to confirm and for counselling. Never delay treatment of a crisis for the confirmatory result. Pheochromocytoma Plasma free metanephrines , drawn supine, or 24-hour urinary fractionated metanephrines Metanephrines are preferred over catecholamines because the tumour metabolizes catecholamines continuously while secreting them episodically — so the metabolites are always elevated whereas the parent hormones may be normal between attacks. Confirm, then image (CT or MRI, with functional imaging if extra-adrenal or metastatic disease is suspected), then refer everyone for genetic testing . Virilization 17-OHP, DHEA-S, androstenedione, testosterone A very high DHEA-S points to the adrenal, a very high testosterone with normal DHEA-S to the gonad, and a high 17-OHP to CAH. Bone age, then imaging directed by the biochemistry. Adrenal incidentaloma 1 mg overnight dexamethasone suppression test + metanephrines (+ ARR if hypertensive or hypokalemic) Characterize on imaging by size and attenuation. Do not biopsy before pheochromocytoma has been excluded. Two numbers, and a caveat about them The slide set gives >2 µg/dL as inadequate suppression on the overnight dexamethasone test. The threshold in wide use, including in the Endocrine Society guidance, is 1.8 µg/dL (50 nmol/L) , chosen deliberately to favour sensitivity — it will call some normal people abnormal, which is the correct trade-off for a screening test that is always followed by a second one. Similarly, the 18 µg/dL post-cosyntropin threshold comes from older cortisol assays; modern specific assays read lower and many centres now use a cut-off in the 14–15 µg/dL range. Know the classic numbers, and know that they are assay-dependent. Nieman LK et al. The Diagnosis of Cushing's Syndrome: An Endocrine Society Clinical Practice Guideline. endocrine.org · Adrenocorticotropic Hormone (Cosyntropin) Stimulation Test. StatPearls. ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/books/NBK555940

entries.title: Management
entries.text: Management Objective 3. Notice how often the level of the lesion — gland, pituitary, or hypothalamus — changes the treatment rather than just the label. Primary aldosteronism unilateral vs bilateral decides everything Surgical or medical Unilateral — an adenoma Laparoscopic adrenalectomy. These tumours are usually under 2 cm. Surgery reliably corrects the hypokalemia and improves, though does not always cure, the hypertension. Bilateral hyperplasia Mineralocorticoid receptor antagonist — spironolactone or eplerenone. Removing one of two overactive glands does not solve a bilateral problem. Glucocorticoid-remediable aldosteronism A low-dose glucocorticoid to suppress the ACTH drive, with or without an MRA. Very rare, but it is the one form where the treatment follows directly from the molecular lesion — see the steroid page . Secondary hyperaldosteronism Treat the cause of the renal hypoperfusion — revascularize the stenosis, manage the heart failure or the cirrhosis. Blocking aldosterone alone addresses a symptom of the real problem. Cushing syndrome treatment follows the source Source-directed Pituitary adenoma — Cushing disease Transsphenoidal resection is first line, with radiation for residual or recurrent disease. Primary adrenal disease Unilateral or bilateral adrenalectomy depending on the lesion. After bilateral adrenalectomy the patient needs lifelong glucocorticoid and mineralocorticoid replacement. Ectopic ACTH Excise the tumour where that is possible. Medical therapy For recurrence, inoperable disease, or to control severe hypercortisolism before surgery: steroidogenesis inhibitors (ketoconazole, metyrapone, osilodrostat), pasireotide acting on the pituitary tumour, and mifepristone , a glucocorticoid receptor antagonist used mainly for the hyperglycemia. Adrenal insufficiency — chronic replacement what you replace depends on the level Lifelong Primary Glucocorticoid and mineralocorticoid. Hydrocortisone in divided doses mimicking the diurnal rhythm, plus fludrocortisone because the zona glomerulosa has been destroyed along with everything else. Infants and small children also need sodium chloride supplementation . Secondary and tertiary Glucocorticoid only. No fludrocortisone is needed, because the adrenal gland and the renin–angiotensin–aldosterone system are both intact — the gland is simply unstimulated. This single difference is the practical reason localization matters. Non-negotiable in both Stress dosing — two to three times the usual dose during febrile illness, and parenteral hydrocortisone for vomiting, trauma, or surgery. An emergency injection kit , written sick-day rules, and medical alert identification . Patients die of untreated crises, not of the underlying diagnosis. Congenital adrenal hyperplasia replace, suppress, and grow the child normally Pediatric The regimen Hydrocortisone for glucocorticoid replacement — preferred in growing children because its short half-life is least suppressive of growth, and it carries useful mineralocorticoid activity at higher doses. Fludrocortisone for the mineralocorticoid arm — note there is no intravenous form , which matters in a vomiting child. Salt supplementation in infancy. The therapeutic target is a balance Enough glucocorticoid to prevent crisis and suppress the androgen drive , not so much that it stunts growth and causes iatrogenic Cushing syndrome . Under-treatment lets androgens advance bone age and shorten adult height; over-treatment does the same thing by a different route. Monitor growth velocity, bone age, 17-OHP, and androstenedione. Pheochromocytoma the order of the drugs is the exam point Sequence matters Alpha blockade first Normalize the blood pressure before anything else , with an α-adrenergic blocker — phenoxybenzamine, or a selective α1 agent such as doxazosin or prazosin — started well ahead of surgery, together with liberal salt and fluid intake to re-expand the contracted plasma volume. Never a beta blocker alone Blocking β receptors while α receptors remain unopposed removes β2-mediated vasodilation and leaves pure α-mediated vasoconstriction — a hypertensive crisis . A beta blocker may be added after adequate α blockade to control reflex tachycardia, never before. Then surgery Surgical excision , which is a high-risk procedure requiring an experienced surgical and anesthetic team because manipulating the tumour releases catecholamines. Afterwards: lifelong biochemical surveillance, because a fifth to a quarter of these tumours behave malignantly.

entries.title: Adrenal crisis
entries.text: Adrenal crisis — the one to know cold Treat first, confirm afterwards An unwell patient with hypotension unresponsive to fluids, hyponatremia, hyperkalemia, and hypoglycemia — particularly a neonate in the second or third week of life, a patient with known adrenal insufficiency who has become ill, or anyone who has recently stopped long-term steroids — is in adrenal crisis until proved otherwise. Draw a cortisol and an ACTH if you can do it in seconds, then give hydrocortisone. Do not wait for the result. Intravenous hydrocortisone — 100 mg in an adult, weight- or surface-area-based in a child — then intravenous fluid resuscitation with saline containing dextrose , correction of the hypoglycemia, treatment of the precipitating illness , and cardiac monitoring for the hyperkalemia. At stress doses hydrocortisone has enough mineralocorticoid activity that fludrocortisone is not needed acutely — which is convenient, since it only exists as a tablet.

entries.title: Retrieval prompts
entries.text: Retrieval prompts Retrieve Why is a patient with secondary adrenal insufficiency not hyperkalemic, and why are they not hyperpigmented? Because ACTH is low, and because aldosterone is not an ACTH-dependent hormone. The zona glomerulosa answers to angiotensin II and potassium, both of which are intact, so aldosterone is preserved and potassium is handled normally — hence no hyperkalemia and no need for fludrocortisone. Hyperpigmentation requires excess ACTH and related POMC peptides acting on melanocortin receptors in skin; with ACTH low there is nothing to drive it. The two findings are the fastest bedside way to say primary or central. Retrieve A patient has a CT showing a 1.5 cm left adrenal nodule and biochemically confirmed primary aldosteronism. Why is adrenal vein sampling still required before surgery? Because CT shows anatomy and the question is function. Non-functioning adrenal nodules are common and become commoner with age, so the visible nodule may be an innocent bystander while the contralateral gland — or both glands — is the source. CT also misses small aldosterone-producing adenomas altogether. Removing the wrong gland leaves the patient with persistent hyperaldosteronism and one fewer adrenal. CT is still done in everyone, but for a different reason: to exclude a large mass suspicious for adrenocortical carcinoma. Retrieve Two children with CAH: one is hypotensive and hyperkalemic, the other is hypertensive and hypokalemic. Name both enzymes and explain the difference. 21-hydroxylase deficiency and 11β-hydroxylase deficiency . The block in 21-hydroxylase deficiency sits above 11-deoxycorticosterone, so no mineralocorticoid of any kind is made and the child salt-wastes. The block in 11β-hydroxylase deficiency sits one step below DOC, so DOC accumulates; it is a weak mineralocorticoid, but in that quantity it retains sodium, raises blood pressure, and wastes potassium. Both children virilize, because in both the accumulated precursor is shunted into the androgen branch. Retrieve Why are metanephrines, rather than catecholamines, the first-line test for pheochromocytoma? Because secretion is episodic but metabolism is continuous. The tumour metabolizes catecholamines to metanephrines inside the tumour cells , around the clock, and leaks the metabolites steadily. So a catecholamine level drawn between paroxysms can be normal, whereas metanephrines stay elevated. That is what gives plasma free metanephrines their very high sensitivity — the property you want in a screening test for a tumour you cannot afford to miss. Retrieve A 21-year-old with prior parathyroidectomy presents with episodic headache and sweating and a blood pressure of 210/109. Which syndrome, and what must happen before any surgery? MEN2A — hyperparathyroidism plus a pheochromocytoma, both from a RET mutation, with medullary thyroid carcinoma to be sought urgently. MEN1 includes hyperparathyroidism but not pheochromocytoma; MEN2B includes pheochromocytoma but not hyperparathyroidism. Before any operation the pheochromocytoma must be diagnosed biochemically and the patient α-blocked and volume-repleted . Anesthesia in an unprepared patient can precipitate a fatal hypertensive crisis, and the thyroid surgery this patient will eventually need must wait behind the adrenal. Practice questions — placeholder Multiple-choice questions for this lecture have not been written yet. When they are added to assets/data/endocrine_question_bank.json with "lecture": "Adrenal Gland Disorders" , they will appear here and in cumulative practice automatically. The in-lecture practice items the slides pose — which stimuli raise aldosterone, what causes Cushing disease, which hormone causes the hypertension of 11β-hydroxylase deficiency, and the MEN2A vignette — are all covered above and would be the natural first four to write.

entries.title: How to read this page
entries.text: What this session asks of you The seven stated objectives, and where each one is answered 1. Why DSDs are a medical and psychosocial emergency in the newborn period → why this is an emergency . 2. The clinical findings that warrant evaluation → when to evaluate . 3. The 46,XX DSDs — CAH, SRY-positive 46,XX, placental aromatase deficiency → 46,XX DSD . 4. The 46,XY DSDs — AMH deficiency, testosterone synthesis and Leydig cell defects, 5α-reductase deficiency, complete and partial androgen insensitivity → 46,XY DSD . 5. The sex chromosome DSDs — complete and mixed gonadal dysgenesis, ovotesticular DSD, Turner, Klinefelter, and Kallmann → sex chromosome DSD . 6. The role of newborn screening in CAH → newborn screening . 7. The current multidisciplinary approach to sex assignment and long-term management → sex assignment and long-term care . A note on the words DSD stands for disorders of sex development in the 2006 Chicago consensus statement that introduced it; differences of sex development is now widely preferred, and many affected people use intersex variation . The consensus replaced intersex , hermaphrodite , and pseudohermaphrodite , which are stigmatizing and should not be used clinically , and grounded the classification in karyotype instead of appearance. You will still meet the old words in older texts and in pathology reports. Sex and gender are not the same thing : this page is about the biology of sex development, and it does not predict gender identity.

entries.title: Normal sexual development
entries.text: Three steps, in order The three sequential steps of sexual development Chromosomal sex is set at conception. Around six weeks after conception the bipotential gonad differentiates: with SRY present on the short arm of the Y chromosome it becomes a testis, and without SRY it becomes an ovary. The testis produces anti-Mullerian hormone from Sertoli cells, which regresses the Mullerian ducts, and testosterone from Leydig cells, which maintains the Wolffian ducts and is converted by 5-alpha-reductase to dihydrotestosterone, which virilizes the external genitalia. Without a testis there is no AMH so the Mullerian ducts persist to form the uterus, tubes and upper vagina, and no testosterone so the Wolffian ducts regress and the external genitalia remain female in appearance. 1 · chromosomal sex bipotential gonad · ~6 weeks post-conception 2 · gonadal sex SRY + no SRY testis ovary 3 · phenotypic Sertoli → AMH Müllerian regress Leydig → testosterone Wolffian maintained no AMH, no testosterone Müllerian stay · Wolffian regress 5α-reductase dihydrotestosterone virilized external genitalia female external genitalia The default is the right-hand column. Producing the left-hand column requires three separate hormonal signals, each of which can fail on its own. Original diagram. Read the three horizontal bands as three independent questions, because that is how the diseases behave. Chromosomal: what karyotype? Gonadal: did a testis form? Phenotypic: were AMH, testosterone, and DHT each delivered and each received? Almost every diagnosis on this page is a single one of those signals failing while the others work — which is why the phenotypes are so specific. Chromosomal sex Determined at conception. The determining element is SRY — the sex-determining region on the short arm of the Y chromosome — which acts as a switch that turns on the Sertoli cell programme. Many other transcription factors participate; SRY is the trigger, not the whole mechanism. Gonadal sex The bipotential gonad differentiates at around six weeks post-conception (the second month). With SRY it becomes a testis ; without SRY it becomes an ovary . Everything downstream depends on which one formed, because the phenotype is driven by hormones the gonad makes. Phenotypic sex Driven by the gonad's output. Internal ducts: both Müllerian and Wolffian systems are present initially and one set regresses. External genitalia: a single bipotential anlage that virilizes if it sees enough DHT. The timing and pattern vary , and that variation is diagnostically useful. The three hormonal signals, and what each one does AMH, from Sertoli cells — regresses the Müllerian ducts, which would otherwise become the uterus, fallopian tubes, and upper two-thirds of the vagina. Acts locally, so a unilateral testis regresses only its own side. Testosterone, from Leydig cells — maintains the Wolffian ducts (epididymis, vas deferens, seminal vesicles). Also acts locally and at high concentration, which is why circulating adrenal androgen cannot substitute for it. DHT, converted from testosterone by 5α-reductase in the target tissue — is the potent virilizer of the external genitalia . Testosterone alone will not do this job, and that single fact explains an entire disease. Timing decides what the virilization looks like In a 46,XX fetus, androgen exposure before 13 weeks of gestation — while the labioscrotal folds are still able to fuse — produces posterior labial fusion and a urogenital sinus. Exposure from about 14 weeks onward , once those structures have already formed, produces clitoromegaly without fusion . So the degree and type of virilization tells you when the androgen arrived, which narrows the differential before any test comes back.

entries.title: Why this is an emergency
entries.text: Why a DSD is both a medical and a psychosocial emergency Objective 1. There are two independent reasons, and they need different responses. The medical emergency Some of these infants are in the first days of a life-threatening endocrine illness . Congenital adrenal hyperplasia — the commonest cause of a 46,XX DSD — produces adrenal crisis at roughly 10 to 21 days of life : vomiting, poor feeding, failure to thrive, dehydration, hyponatremia, hyperkalemia, hypoglycemia, and shock . The infant looks well at birth. Panhypopituitarism is the other one to fear, presenting with hypoglycemia and micropenis. Both are treatable and both are lethal untreated, which is what makes the evaluation urgent rather than merely thorough. The psychosocial emergency "Is it a boy or a girl?" is the first question anyone asks about a newborn, and the family cannot answer it. The consequences are real: acute distress and anxiety in the parents , disruption of bonding with the infant, pressure from relatives, and decisions made under time pressure that are irreversible . The response is not speed for its own sake — it is rapid, coordinated evaluation with honest ongoing communication , so that the family is never left without information and never pushed into an early decision. How the team communicates while the workup runs Use neutral anatomical language — clitorophallus , labioscrotal folds , gonads — rather than sex-specific terms, and avoid pronouns until sex of rearing is agreed. Do not guess , and do not offer a provisional answer that may have to be retracted. Involve the parents in an informed discussion from the beginning rather than presenting them with conclusions. And the team must speak with one consensus voice : contradictory statements from different specialists are one of the most damaging things that can happen to a family in this situation. Scale DSDs occur in roughly 1 in 4,500 to 5,500 live births taken together — uncommon individually, and collectively something any pediatrician or family physician will meet.

entries.title: When to evaluate
entries.text: The findings that warrant evaluation Objective 2. Note that several of these occur in an infant whose genitalia look unremarkable at a glance. External genital findings Apparent female: clitoromegaly, posterior labial fusion, a single perineal opening (urogenital sinus), or an inguinal or labial mass , which may be a testis. Apparent male: bilateral non-palpable gonads , severe hypospadias — particularly perineal or penoscrotal — hypospadias with undescended testis , micropenis , and a bifid scrotum . Frankly ambiguous genitalia in either direction. Findings away from the genitalia Signs of adrenal insufficiency — poor feeding, vomiting, failure to thrive, dehydration, hypotension, hyperpigmentation of the genital skin and areolae, hypoglycemia, hyponatremia with hyperkalemia. Associated congenital anomalies , since several DSDs are syndromic. A discordance between prenatal karyotype and the appearance at birth . And a family history of DSD, consanguinity, unexplained neonatal death, or infertility. One physical sign carries more weight than any other A palpable gonad is almost always a testis. Ovaries do not descend. So a palpable gonad in the labioscrotal fold or the inguinal canal means testicular tissue is present, which immediately makes a 46,XX DSD unlikely and reorients the workup toward undervirilization of a 46,XY infant, ovotesticular DSD, or gonadal dysgenesis. Symmetry matters too: symmetric findings suggest a hormonal cause, asymmetric findings suggest dysgenesis . Bilaterally non-palpable gonads in an apparently male infant should be treated as CAH until excluded — that infant may be a virilized 46,XX girl heading for a salt-wasting crisis.

entries.title: The workup
entries.text: The workup Examination, documented precisely Phallic length and diameter. Labioscrotal folds — fused or not, and how far posteriorly. Position of the urethral meatus. Anogenital ratio. Palpable gonads — present or absent, and on which side. Hyperpigmentation , which points to high ACTH and therefore to CAH. Plus a general examination for dysmorphic features and other anomalies. First-line laboratory studies Karyotype — with FISH for SRY where relevant — as the first branch point. 17-hydroxyprogesterone , because CAH is the diagnosis that cannot wait. Serum electrolytes and glucose , followed serially through the first two weeks. Testosterone, DHT, AMH, LH and FSH , and further steroid precursors as the pattern directs. Imaging Pelvic and abdominal ultrasound first: is there a uterus , are there intra-abdominal or streak gonads , is there adrenal hyperplasia . Genitogram to define a urogenital sinus and the anatomy of the vagina and urethra. MRI or CT of the abdomen and pelvis when the ultrasound leaves questions open. Who is on the team A coordinated group, assembled at once rather than sequentially: neonatology or general pediatrics , endocrinology , urology , pediatric surgery , gynecology , genetics , and psychology or mental health . Social work and ethics support where available. The team's most important operational rule is the one already stated — speak with one voice .

entries.title: Classification
entries.text: Classification: karyotype first The 2006 consensus classification. Categorizing by karyotype rather than by appearance is the point of it — appearance is what you are trying to explain, so it cannot also be the organizing principle. 46,XX DSD — over-virilization 46,XY DSD — under-virilization Sex chromosome DSD Androgen excess: congenital adrenal hyperplasia , placental aromatase deficiency , maternal sources (luteoma, exogenous androgen) Disorders of androgen synthesis : testosterone synthesis defects , Leydig cell hypoplasia or LH-receptor defects , 5α-reductase deficiency Turner syndrome (45,X and variants) Disorders of ovarian development: SRY-positive 46,XX testicular DSD , ovotesticular DSD Disorders of androgen responsiveness : complete and partial androgen insensitivity Klinefelter syndrome (47,XXY and variants) Other: vaginal atresia, cloacal exstrophy, Müllerian agenesis Disorders of testicular development, and AMH deficiency 45,X/46,XY mixed gonadal dysgenesis · 46,XX/46,XY chimerism

entries.title: 46,XX DSD
entries.text: 46,XX DSD — the over-virilized Objective 3. Ovaries, a uterus, and a fetus that saw androgen it should not have seen. Congenital adrenal hyperplasia the commonest DSD, and the dangerous one Emergency Pathophysiology Autosomal recessive ; an inborn error of cortisol and aldosterone production, over 90% of cases from 21-hydroxylase deficiency . Low cortisol removes feedback, ACTH rises, the adrenals become hyperplastic, and the accumulated precursor is shunted into the androgen branch . The full derivation is on the steroid synthesis page . Presentation A 46,XX infant with atypical genitalia — clitoromegaly, labioscrotal fusion, a urogenital sinus — and no palpable gonads , because the ovaries are intra-abdominal. Internal structures (uterus, tubes, ovaries) are normal . Then, in the salt-wasting form, adrenal crisis at 10–21 days : failure to thrive, progressive weight loss, dehydration, high potassium, low sodium, low cortisol, shock . Hyperpigmentation of the genital skin is a useful early clue. Evaluation 17-hydroxyprogesterone — markedly raised. Karyotype 46,XX. Ultrasound shows a uterus and often hyperplastic adrenals . Electrolytes and glucose, repeated: the crisis develops over days and a normal sodium on day 2 means nothing on day 12. Why this one is first on every list It is both the commonest cause of a 46,XX DSD and the only cause of atypical genitalia that is immediately life-threatening . Every newborn genital-anomaly workup is built around excluding it first. Frequency is usually quoted at roughly 1 in 15,000 births for the classic form. Placental aromatase deficiency CYP19A1 — the one where the mother virilizes too Distinctive clue Pathophysiology Aromatase normally converts fetal androgens to estrogens in the placenta, protecting both fetus and pregnant person from androgen exposure. In its absence — biallelic CYP19A1 variants, autosomal recessive — those androgens cross unchanged. Presentation Both the baby and the pregnant person virilize. Maternal acne, hirsutism, and voice change appear during the pregnancy, often from the second trimester, and regress after delivery . The 46,XX infant has atypical genitalia ranging from clitoromegaly to complete labioscrotal fusion. Later: absent puberty with tall stature, ovarian cysts, delayed bone age and low bone density from estrogen deficiency. How it is distinguished from CAH Maternal virilization is the discriminator , because in CAH the mother is unaffected. Biochemically, 17-OHP is normal , and estrogens are low with high androgens. A maternal luteoma or exogenous androgen exposure produces a similar fetal picture and is excluded by history. SRY-positive 46,XX testicular DSD a male phenotype with an XX karyotype Translocation Pathophysiology During paternal meiosis, SRY translocates onto an X chromosome . The resulting 46,XX embryo receives the testis-determining signal, so the bipotential gonad becomes a testis and the phenotype develops along male lines. About 80% of nonsyndromic 46,XX testicular DSD is SRY-positive ; the remainder involve other genes in the same pathway. Presentation Usually a phenotypic male , sometimes with hypospadias or small testes. Many are not identified until adolescence or adult infertility work-up. Because the rest of the Y — including the azoospermia factor region — is absent, there is azoospermia and infertility , and testosterone often falls short at puberty with a compensatory rise in gonadotropins. Evaluation Karyotype 46,XX with a FISH probe positive for SRY (or chromosomal microarray). Incidence is on the order of 1 in 20,000 . Long-term care is testosterone replacement if needed, and fertility counselling.

entries.title: 46,XY DSD
entries.text: 46,XY DSD — the under-virilized Objective 4. A testis formed. Something after that failed — production, conversion, or reception. Sort them by which of the three signals failed AMH failed → Müllerian structures persist in an otherwise male infant. Testosterone production failed → both duct systems and the external genitalia are underdeveloped. Conversion to DHT failed → internal male structures are present, external genitalia are not virilized. Reception failed → nothing androgen-dependent forms at all, but AMH still worked, so there is no uterus. That last contrast — no androgen effect with no Müllerian structures — is the fingerprint of androgen insensitivity. AMH deficiency persistent Müllerian duct syndrome Signal 1 failed Pathophysiology Absent AMH production or a defective AMH receptor . The Sertoli cells fail to deliver the regression signal, so the Müllerian ducts persist . Leydig cell function is normal, so testosterone is made and the Wolffian structures are also present — this is the one condition where both duct systems coexist. Presentation Phenotypically male external genitalia , with undescended testes — the Müllerian remnants tether them. Inguinal hernia is common , and the diagnosis is classically made at hernia repair or orchiopexy when a uterus and tubes are found unexpectedly. Management Orchiopexy to retrieve the testes and place them in the scrotum, with careful handling of the Müllerian remnants and the vas, which run close together. Long-term concerns are fertility and the malignancy risk that accompanies cryptorchidism. Defects of testosterone synthesis including Leydig cell and LH-receptor defects Signal 2 failed Pathophysiology A defect can sit at almost every step of the pathway from cholesterol to testosterone — StAR, CYP11A1, 3β-HSD, CYP17A1, 17β-HSD — or in the Leydig cell itself , through hypoplasia or an inactivating LH-receptor mutation. Where the block is high in the pathway the adrenal steroids are affected too and there is accompanying adrenal insufficiency. Presentation Undervirilization of a 46,XY infant , along a spectrum from mild hypospadias to entirely female-appearing external genitalia. There is no uterus , because AMH is unaffected. Wolffian development is variable and follows how much testosterone was actually made. The useful test, and the treatment These infants respond to testosterone therapy , and that response is diagnostically informative — it separates a synthesis defect from androgen insensitivity, where exogenous testosterone does nothing. Precursor-to-product ratios locate the specific block. 5α-reductase deficiency SRD5A2 — testosterone made, DHT not Signal 3 failed Pathophysiology Autosomal recessive loss of 5α-reductase type 2, so testosterone is not converted to DHT in the genital skin. Testosterone maintains the Wolffian ducts perfectly well; DHT is what virilizes the external genitalia, and it is missing. Presentation at birth Minimal external male development : an enlarged clitorophallus, an incomplete scrotum, undescended testes, a perineal urethral opening — while internal "male" ducts are present and there is no uterus. Many are assigned female at birth. Presentation at puberty The large pubertal rise in testosterone acts directly on the androgen receptor and produces virilization : increased muscle mass, increased phallic size, deepening voice, onset of erections. This is the phenomenon described in the Dominican Republic cohorts as "guevedoce" , where the local prevalence has been reported as high as 1 in 90 male births in an affected community. Evaluation A raised testosterone-to-DHT ratio , particularly after hCG stimulation, plus SRD5A2 genotyping . The prospect of virilization at puberty is a central consideration in sex-of-rearing discussions, and one of the strongest arguments for not performing irreversible surgery in infancy. Androgen insensitivity syndrome complete (CAIS) and partial (PAIS) Receptor defect Pathophysiology An X-linked defect of the androgen receptor . Androgen biosynthesis is entirely normal — the hormone is there and the tissue cannot hear it. AMH is unaffected , so the Müllerian ducts still regress: no uterus, no tubes, no upper vagina . The Wolffian ducts, which need androgen, do not develop. CAIS Phenotypically female external genitalia with a short blind-ending vaginal pouch and no uterus . Testes are intra-abdominal or inguinal — sometimes presenting as an inguinal hernia in an apparently female infant. Little or no axillary and pubic hair , because that hair is androgen-dependent. Testosterone is normal for the male reference range. Breast development at puberty is normal, because testosterone aromatizes to estrogen and there is no androgen opposition. The usual presentation is primary amenorrhea in an otherwise typically developing adolescent. PAIS A spectrum , from a phenotypic female with mild virilization through frankly ambiguous genitalia to an undervirilized male with hypospadias, micropenis, or gynecomastia. Management is correspondingly individualized and considerably harder than in CAIS. Long-term care Estrogen replacement after gonadectomy, vaginal management where needed, psychological support, and a discussion about gonadal malignancy risk and the timing of gonadectomy — the modern approach is to defer, since the risk in CAIS is low before puberty and the gonads provide the estrogen that drives normal pubertal development. Gottlieb B, Trifiro MA. Androgen Insensitivity Syndrome. GeneReviews. ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/books/NBK1429 · 5α-Reductase Deficiency. StatPearls. ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/books/NBK539904

entries.title: Sex chromosome DSD
entries.text: Sex chromosome DSD Objective 5. Here the first step — chromosomal sex — is itself atypical, so the gonad is the structure that suffers. Ovotesticular DSD formerly "true hermaphroditism" — a term no longer used Both tissues Definition Both ovarian and testicular tissue in the same individual. The possible arrangements are two ovotestes ; one ovotestis with an ovary or a testis ; one ovary and one testis; or one ovotestis and one streak gonad . Presentation Highly variable , because the phenotype depends on how much functioning testicular tissue there is and where it sits. Both Müllerian and Wolffian structures or remnants are typically present, often asymmetrically — a Müllerian structure on the ovarian side where no local AMH was produced. Karyotype and frequency A variety of chromosomal patterns ; the commonest in most reported series is 46,XX , with 46,XX/46,XY chimerism and 46,XY also described. It is uncommon — under 10% of DSD in the United States. Mixed gonadal dysgenesis A streak gonad on one side and a testis (or ovary) on the other. A streak is an underdeveloped, non-functional gonad replaced by fibrous connective tissue. The karyotype is usually mosaic — 45,X/46,XY , sometimes 46,XX/46,XY. The phenotype varies widely and is characteristically asymmetric , which is the physical clue. Because Y-derived material sits in a dysgenetic gonad , the risk of gonadoblastoma is substantial — reported at roughly 15–25% — and gonadal management and surveillance are part of the plan. Complete (pure) gonadal dysgenesis Bilateral streak gonads , usually with a 46,XX karyotype, sometimes 45,X — and the 46,XY form is Swyer syndrome. Because there is no AMH and no testosterone , the phenotype is female, internally and externally , including a uterus. The presentation is therefore delayed or absent puberty with gonadal failure and high gonadotropins, not genital ambiguity. Malignancy risk is not increased unless Y chromosome material is present — and where it is, the risk again approaches 25%, which is what drives the recommendation for gonadectomy in that group. Turner syndrome 45,X and variants Short stature + ovarian failure Genetics Complete or partial absence of the second sex chromosome ; 45,X is the commonest single karyotype, with mosaics and structural X abnormalities making up much of the rest. Loss of one copy of SHOX accounts for the short stature. Reported in roughly 1 in 2,000 to 2,500 live female births . The two near-universal features Short stature and ovarian failure . The gonads are streaks, so estrogen is absent and LH and FSH are high — hypergonadotropic hypogonadism. Expect delayed or absent puberty, premature ovarian insufficiency, and infertility . The rest of the phenotype Neonatal lymphedema of the hands and feet, webbed neck , low posterior hairline, left-sided cardiac anomalies — bicuspid aortic valve and coarctation, with aortic dissection the feared complication — renal anomalies , and orthopedic anomalies. Also hearing loss, hypothyroidism, and specific learning differences. The presentation to recognize A short girl with delayed puberty , often with a cardiac anomaly already known. Any girl with unexplained short stature or primary amenorrhea deserves a karyotype. Klinefelter syndrome 47,XXY and variants Tall + small firm testes Genetics One or more extra X chromosomes — 47,XXY most often, with 48,XXXY and higher-grade variants producing more severe phenotypes. Among the commonest chromosomal conditions, generally quoted at around 1 in 500 to 1,000 male births , and substantially under-diagnosed. The endocrine lesion Primary testicular failure. The seminiferous tubules degenerate and are replaced by hyaline, giving small, firm testes and azoospermia . Leydig cell function is also impaired, so testosterone is low while LH and FSH are high — hypergonadotropic hypogonadism, the same pattern as Turner syndrome and for the same reason. The phenotype that follows Low androgen means poor muscle development , a more typically female fat distribution, gynecomastia , and sparse facial hair — although pubic and axillary hair are often normal, since adrenal androgen covers that. Tall stature , attributed to the extra SHOX copy and to delayed epiphyseal closure. Eunuchoid proportions. Learning and language differences are common. The presentation to recognize A tall adolescent male with delayed or stalled puberty and small testes , with high LH and FSH and low testosterone . Management is testosterone replacement and fertility counselling — sperm retrieval is sometimes possible. Kallmann syndrome not a DSD — a cause of hypogonadism, included for contrast Contrast case Mechanism GnRH neurons fail to migrate from the olfactory placode to the hypothalamus during development. Because those neurons travel with the olfactory axons, the same failure costs both. Genes include ANOS1/KAL1 (X-linked), FGFR1, CHD7, PROK2, and PROKR2. Presentation Hypogonadotropic hypogonadism plus anosmia. Delayed puberty with absent testicular development, or primary amenorrhea. Micropenis and cryptorchidism may be present at birth. Why it sits at the end of this list It is the opposite biochemical pattern to Turner and Klinefelter: low LH and FSH with low sex steroids — the signal is missing, not the gonad. The karyotype is normal , which is why it is not truly a DSD. Diagnosis: low gonadotropins with low testosterone or estradiol, MRI showing hypoplastic or absent olfactory bulbs , and genetic testing. Treatment is sex steroid replacement, with gonadotropin therapy when fertility is the goal.

entries.title: Newborn screening for CAH
entries.text: Newborn screening for congenital adrenal hyperplasia Objective 6, and the clearest example on this page of a screening programme designed around one specific failure mode. How it detects classic CAH A heel-stick dried blood spot is assayed for 17-hydroxyprogesterone , the precursor immediately above the 21-hydroxylase block. In classic CAH it is markedly elevated — values in the thousands of ng/dL against a normal of tens. A positive screen triggers same-day confirmatory serum testing and electrolytes. Why salt-wasting CAH needs urgent diagnosis Because the crisis arrives at 10 to 21 days of life in an infant who was well at birth and discharged home . Untreated it is hyponatremia, hyperkalemia, hypoglycemia, hypovolemic shock, and death . There is no window for a leisurely workup: the screen has to find these infants before the crisis, not during it. Why male infants are the target A 46,XX infant with classic CAH is virilized at birth , so the genital findings themselves prompt evaluation. A 46,XY infant looks completely normal — there is nothing to see, no reason to test, and the first sign is the crisis. Newborn screening exists primarily to catch that infant. Its second benefit is preventing incorrect sex assignment of a severely virilized 46,XX infant. The cost of the design, stated honestly The cut-off is set low, deliberately, to maximize sensitivity — missing a case means a dead infant, so the programme accepts a great many false positives to avoid that. The consequence is poor specificity and a high false-positive rate , and the false positives are concentrated in preterm, sick, and physiologically stressed infants , in whom 17-OHP is elevated for entirely benign reasons. That is why gestational-age-adjusted cut-offs are used, why a second-tier assay is increasingly added, and why a positive screen is a reason to test, not a diagnosis .

entries.title: Work the cases
entries.text: Karyotype, gonads, and the first labs Ten cases spanning all three categories. Work each one before reading the explanation. The algorithm underneath those cases Step 1 — karyotype. It splits the differential into the three columns of the classification table. Step 2 — palpable gonads, and symmetry. Palpable means testicular tissue; asymmetry means dysgenesis. Step 3 — 17-hydroxyprogesterone and electrolytes. This is the step that finds the infant who is about to become critically unwell, and it happens in parallel with the other two rather than after them. Step 4 — is there a uterus on ultrasound? A uterus means AMH was never delivered; no uterus means it was. Step 5 — the hormone axis. Testosterone, DHT and their ratio, AMH, LH and FSH: high gonadotropins with low sex steroids localizes to the gonad, low gonadotropins with low sex steroids localizes above it.

entries.title: Sex assignment
entries.text: Sex assignment and long-term management Objective 7. This is where the field has changed most, and the exam question is usually about why it changed. The traditional paradigm, and what it got right Developed in the 1950s by John Money and Lawson Wilkins . It was deeply critical of assigning sex on any single criterion — not on chromosomes alone, not on gonads alone — and it insisted on a thorough workup : identify the etiology, assess what interventions are possible, and choose the option most congruent with anticipated development at puberty and in adulthood. Those parts have survived. Where it went wrong was the final step: early "normalizing" genital surgery , performed to remove parental doubt and, it was believed, to enable gender identity to develop properly. Why that final step was abandoned The claim was empirical, and it did not hold up. There is no evidence that early feminizing genital surgery improves psychosocial outcome , and there is increasing evidence of harm — from small studies, long-term follow-up, and patient testimony: loss of sexual function and sensation, repeated operations, and distress where the assigned sex did not match the person's eventual gender identity. The asymmetry that settles the argument is stated on the slide in seven words: sex assignment is reversible, surgery is not . The questions the team asks now Who is the patient? The infant — not the parents, however genuine their distress. Is this treatment medically necessary? Distinguish interventions needed for health (relieving urinary obstruction, treating adrenal insufficiency, managing malignancy risk) from those performed for appearance. Can it wait? If it can be deferred safely, defer it. Until when? Until gender identity is established and the person can participate in the decision, keeping in mind that gender identity may not match the sex assigned in infancy. The patient-centered paradigm, in six commitments Treat the medical issues — adrenal insufficiency, hypoglycemia, obstruction, malignancy risk — promptly and fully. Do not forcibly normalize. Avoid stigmatizing language, examinations, and photography. Elective surgical and hormonal interventions should be chosen by the patient when they are able to choose. Address psychosocial distress directly , with mental health professionals as core team members rather than an afterthought. Always tell the truth — to the family throughout, and to the patient in an age-appropriate way as they grow. Concealment was standard practice for decades and is one of the harms patients report most consistently. What still has to be decided early Deferring surgery is not the same as deferring everything. A sex of rearing is still assigned , after full evaluation and in partnership with the family, because a child needs one to live in the world — and it is chosen using diagnosis, expected pubertal course, fertility potential, and the outcome data for that specific condition. Some decisions genuinely cannot wait: glucocorticoid and mineralocorticoid replacement in CAH , gonadal malignancy surveillance where Y material is present in a dysgenetic gonad , and relief of urinary obstruction . The principle is not "do nothing" — it is do what is necessary now, and leave what is elective to the person it belongs to . Lee PA, Houk CP, Ahmed SF, Hughes IA. Consensus statement on management of intersex disorders. Pediatrics 2006;118(2):e488–500 — the Chicago consensus, source of the current nomenclature and classification.

entries.title: Retrieval prompts
entries.text: Retrieval prompts Retrieve Two 46,XY adolescents present with a female phenotype and primary amenorrhea. One has no uterus and normal male testosterone; the other has a uterus and streak gonads. Name both conditions. Complete androgen insensitivity and 46,XY complete gonadal dysgenesis (Swyer syndrome) . The uterus is the discriminator, and it tells you whether a functioning testis ever existed. In CAIS a testis formed and made AMH, so the Müllerian ducts regressed — no uterus — while the androgen receptor defect prevented any androgen effect. In complete gonadal dysgenesis no testis formed at all, so there was neither AMH nor testosterone: the Müllerian ducts persisted into a uterus and tubes, and the gonads are streaks. Testosterone separates them too — normal male range in CAIS, undetectable in dysgenesis. Retrieve Why does 5α-reductase deficiency spare the internal male ducts but not the external genitalia? Because the two tissues need different hormones. The Wolffian ducts are maintained by testosterone itself, which is made normally. The external genitalia require conversion to dihydrotestosterone in the target tissue, which is the step that is missing. So the epididymis, vas, and seminal vesicles are present while the external genitalia are not virilized — and there is still no uterus, because AMH was never affected. At puberty the sheer size of the testosterone surge produces partial virilization by acting directly on the receptor. Retrieve A newborn appears male with bilaterally non-palpable gonads. What is the first thing you must exclude, and why? Congenital adrenal hyperplasia in a severely virilized 46,XX infant. Ovaries do not descend, so bilaterally non-palpable gonads in an apparently male infant should raise the possibility that this is not a male infant at all. Two things follow: the sex of rearing may be wrong, and — far more urgently — that infant is on a trajectory toward a salt-wasting adrenal crisis at 10 to 21 days . Send a karyotype and a 17-hydroxyprogesterone, and follow electrolytes and glucose over the first two weeks rather than checking them once. Retrieve Give the three gonadotropin patterns and what each localizes to. High LH/FSH with low sex steroids — hypergonadotropic hypogonadism: the gonad has failed and feedback is lost. Turner syndrome, Klinefelter syndrome, gonadal dysgenesis. Low LH/FSH with low sex steroids — hypogonadotropic hypogonadism: the signal is missing, and the gonad was never asked. Kallmann syndrome, hypopituitarism, functional causes. Normal-to-high LH with normal male testosterone in a phenotypic female: the hormone is present and the tissue cannot respond — androgen insensitivity. Reading the trophic hormone against the target hormone works here exactly as it does in the thyroid and adrenal axes. Retrieve Newborn screening for CAH has a false-positive rate that would be unacceptable in most other tests. Defend the design. Because the two errors are not equivalent. A false positive costs a repeat blood test and a few days of family anxiety. A false negative costs an infant who was discharged well and dies of an unrecognized salt-wasting crisis in the third week of life — one that is entirely preventable with hydrocortisone, fludrocortisone, saline, and dextrose. When the cost of missing a case is that asymmetric, you set the cut-off for sensitivity and accept the specificity you get. It also explains why preterm and sick infants generate most of the false positives, and why gestational-age-adjusted cut-offs and second-tier assays are used to claw specificity back without giving up sensitivity.
